p.x:
On Sunday, I made pancakes with my dad. First, we put on our aprons. Then we put flour, milk and eggs in a big bowl. We mixed them together.
Dad put some butter in a pan and heated it on the cooker. We poured a little of the mixture into the hot pan. After one minute, Dad turned the pancake over. It was golden and smelled delicious!
We didn't use the oven or the toaster. We ate the pancakes with honey and fruit. My mum said they were the best pancakes ever!

Last month, I joined a cooking class. Our teacher, Chef Lek, taught us some simple rules.
First, prepare everything before you start. Chop the vegetables, measure the sugar with a teaspoon, and weigh the flour on the scales. Set a timer so you don't forget anything on the stove. Many students burnt their first dish because they were looking at their phones!
Next, she taught us about texture. Fried chicken should be crispy on the outside and juicy inside. If you cover it while it's hot, the steam makes it soggy. Meat cooked slowly becomes tender. For salads, she mixed oil, vinegar, salt and pepper to make a simple dressing.
In the baking lesson, we made bread. We mixed flour, water and yeast to make dough. Then we had to knead it for ten minutes, which was hard work! We also learned to separate an egg yolk from the white and whisk the whites until they were stiff. Chef Lek used a blender to make a sauce and showed us how to grate cheese and lemon peel. She reminded us to defrost frozen meat in the fridge, not on the table. At the end, she laughed and said, "In Thailand, the most important tool is the rice cooker!"

Every time we cook, we are performing a series of chemical reactions. Heat changes the structure of food, altering its taste, texture and colour. When bread is toasted or meat is browned, the surface undergoes the Maillard reaction, in which proteins and sugars combine at high temperatures to produce hundreds of new flavour compounds. This explains why a grilled steak tastes so different from a boiled one. Sugar on its own behaves differently: when heated, it melts and begins to caramelise, turning brown and developing a rich, slightly bitter taste.
Starch, the main carbohydrate in rice, potatoes and flour, also changes with heat. When starch is cooked in water, its granules absorb liquid and swell, which is why rice softens and sauces thicken. As a sauce simmers, water evaporates, concentrating its flavour.
Some of the most familiar foods depend on chemistry. Mayonnaise is an emulsion, a mixture of oil and liquid that normally would not combine, held together by molecules in egg yolk. Salt and sugar dissolve in liquid, spreading their flavour evenly. Acidic ingredients such as lime juice and vinegar can even "cook" raw fish without heat by changing its proteins.
Scientists have also identified umami, the savoury fifth taste found in fish sauce, mushrooms and soy sauce, alongside sweet, salty, sour and bitter. Understanding this science is not only interesting but also important for safety: undercooked meat may contain dangerous bacteria, which are destroyed only at sufficiently high temperatures.
